title: God alone is pure act: real being divides into actual, potential, and mixed
pass_a_gloss: Article III. Is-brought-forward Third division of-Being real, and is-explained how GOD is act pure. 1. Thirdly is-divided being real, into that which merely is actual, that which merely is potential, and that which is partly actual, partly potential, or from potency and act mixed. Being merely potential, is that which in-act not exists, but to-exist is-able: such being is rose in winter. To-be-noted here is, Philosophers everywhere to-say, those beings which in-act not exist, but really to-exist are-able, to-be in potency objective: object for of-potency productive which in-causes is-in, is that which from causes is producible, or that which from causes existence not-yet has-received, but to-receive is-able. Being therefore some possible, as-long-as not in-act exists, is object of-potency productive of-causes, and-therefore is-said to-be in potency objective, because namely it-has that potency, which belongs-to things as-long-as they-are objects of-potency of-some causative. Where truly that being in-act produced is, and existence has-received from causes, not longer is object of-potency productive of-causes, and on-that-account is-said not to-be in potency objective. 2. Being merely actual, or act pure, is GOD glorious, to-whom this supreme and perfect actuality is-ascribed: first, to indicating his simplicity: to-him for is-repugnant every composition from potency and act; that is, from principle some potential or imperfect, and principle actual; this is, actuating and perfecting that other principle, as later we-will-declare in doctrine about GOD. Second, to removing and excluding every potency, which imperfection some argues. Three moreover are of-potencies kinds, which on-account-of imperfection their to-GOD to-be-ascribed are-not-able: namely potency objective, which nothing is other, than of-thing producibility from causes its: second, potency passive, which to-things belongs insofar-as they-are-able from agent some to-suffer and to-be-changed: third, potency toward not to-be. First potency is of-things not existing, and-therefore to-GOD who necessarily exists, nor ever was-able not to-exist, to-be-ascribed is-not-able; two later are of-things existing indeed, but mutable and passible: GOD moreover is immutable, and impassible. But of-potency active far other is reason, for potency active, as well have-observed Metaphysicians, rather of-virtue or faculty name deserves, than of-potency: for each-thing acts insofar-as it-is in act, whence itself power of-acting actuality certain is. But will-ask someone: every potency is than-its act more-imperfect: whatever moreover is imperfect, either absolutely, or comparatively, from GOD to-be-removed is. It-is-answered, potency even active in creatures oftentimes to-be more-imperfect than-its act, and-that because of-creature perfection in operation and exercise of-potency is placed, and-is more-perfect when it-acts, than when not it-acts: but GOD not thus himself has, his for supreme and infinite perfection, or beatitude, in this is placed, that he-is GOD, and-therefore not better or more-perfectly himself has, when he-acts, than when not he-acts. 3. Being consisting from potency and act, is Being finite in-act existing in world: is-said moreover of-this-sort being, to-consist from act and potency, or to-be partly actual, partly potential, on-account-of two reasons: First, because in beings finite various are-found compositions, namely from genus and difference, from matter and form, from parts integral, from essence and existence; from essence existing and subsistence to-it superadded, from subject and accident. In all moreover these compositions, (that alone excepted which is from parts integrating) is one principle potential and receptive, which on-that-account is-called potency, other actual and perfective, which on-that-account is-called act: of-former kind principle in every composition is-laid-under, and of-latter kind principle to-it is-superadded. Hence it-is-plain beings finite rightly to-be-said composed from potency and act. Second reason is this: Beings finite, although in-act they-exist, and thus some act and perfection they-have, not nevertheless are merely actual and perfect, but they-have three those of-potencies kinds imperfection arguing. First for before they-exist, they-have objective that potency toward existing. Second when they-exist, they-have potency passive, and receptive of-new accidents. Third, they-have potency toward not to-be: they-are-able for from first cause to-be-abolished, and into nothing to-be-reduced.

pass_b_english: Article III. The third division of real being is set out, and it is explained how God is pure act.

1. Third, real being is divided into that which is merely actual, that which is merely potential, and that which is partly actual, partly potential — or mixed from potency and act. Merely potential being is that which does not exist in act, but can exist: such a being is a rose in winter. It is to be noted here that philosophers commonly say that those beings which do not exist in act, but can really exist, are in objective potency. For the object of the productive potency which is in causes is that which is producible by the causes — or that which has not yet received existence from the causes, but can receive it. Therefore some possible being, so long as it does not exist in act, is the object of the productive potency of causes, and for that reason is said to be in objective potency, because namely it has that potency which belongs to things so long as they are objects of some causative potency. But when that being has been produced in act and has received existence from causes, it is no longer the object of the productive potency of causes, and on that account is said not to be in objective potency.

2. Merely actual being, or pure act, is the glorious God, to whom this supreme and perfect actuality is ascribed: first, to mark his simplicity. For every composition from potency and act is repugnant to him — that is, from some potential or imperfect principle, and an actual principle; that is, one that actuates and perfects that other principle, as we shall later declare in the doctrine concerning God. Second, to remove and exclude every potency that argues some imperfection. Now there are three kinds of potencies which, on account of their imperfection, cannot be ascribed to God: namely objective potency, which is nothing other than the producibility of a thing by its causes; second, passive potency, which belongs to things insofar as they can suffer and be changed by some agent; third, potency toward non-being. The first potency belongs to things that do not exist, and therefore cannot be ascribed to God, who exists necessarily and never could fail to exist; the two latter belong to things that do exist, yet are mutable and passible: but God is immutable and impassible. But of active potency the account is far otherwise. For active potency, as the metaphysicians have well observed, rather deserves the name of virtue or faculty than of potency: for each thing acts insofar as it is in act, whence the very power of acting is a certain actuality. But someone will ask: every potency is more imperfect than its act; and whatever is imperfect, whether absolutely or comparatively, is to be removed from God. It is answered that even active potency in creatures is often more imperfect than its act, and that because the perfection of a creature is placed in the operation and exercise of the potency, and it is more perfect when it acts than when it does not act: but God does not stand thus. For his supreme and infinite perfection, or beatitude, is placed in this — that he is God — and therefore he does not stand better or more perfectly when he acts than when he does not act.

3. Being that consists of potency and act is finite being actually existing in the world. And a being of this sort is said to consist of act and potency, or to be partly actual, partly potential, for two reasons. First, because in finite beings various compositions are found: namely from genus and difference, from matter and form, from integral parts, from essence and existence; from existing essence and subsistence superadded to it, from subject and accident. Now in all these compositions (that alone excepted which is from integrating parts) there is one potential and receptive principle, which on that account is called potency, and another actual and perfective principle, which on that account is called act: the principle of the former kind underlies in every composition, and the principle of the latter kind is superadded to it. Hence it is plain that finite beings are rightly said to be composed of potency and act. The second reason is this: finite beings, although they exist in act and thus have some act and perfection, are nevertheless not merely actual and perfect, but have those three kinds of potencies that argue imperfection. For first, before they exist, they have that objective potency toward existing. Second, when they exist, they have passive potency, and a receptive potency for new accidents. Third, they have potency toward non-being: for they can be abolished by the first cause and reduced to nothing.
source_text:
ART. III.
Affertur Tertia divisio Entis realis, & explicatur quomodo DEUS sit actus purus.

1. Tertio dividitur ens reale, in illud quod mere est actuale, illud quod mere est potentiale, & illud quod est partim actuale, partim potentiale, seu ex potentia & actu mixtum. Ens mere potentiale, est illud quod actu non existit, sed existere potest: tale ens est rosa in hyeme. Notandum hic est, Philosophos passim dicere, ea entia quae actu non existunt, sed realiter existere possunt, esse in potentia objectiva: objectum enim potentiae productivae quae causis inest, est id quod a causis est producibile, seu id quod a causis existentiam nondum accepit, sed accipere potest. Ens igitur aliquod possibile, quamdiu non actu existit, est objectum potentiae productivae causarum, ideoque dicitur esse in potentia objectiva, quia videlicet habet eam potentiam, quae competit rebus quamdiu sunt objecta potentiae alicujus causativae. Ubi vero illud ens actu productum est, & existentiam accepit a causis, non amplius est objectum potentiae productivae causarum, & ob id dicitur non esse in potentia objectiva.

2. Ens mere actuale, seu actus purus, est DEUS gloriosus, cui haec summa & perfecta actualitas tribuitur: primo, ad indicandam ejus simplicitatem: ei enim repugnat omnis compositio ex potentia & actu; id est, ex principio aliquo potentiali vel imperfecto, & principio actuali; hoc est, actuante & perficiente illud alterum principium, ut postea declarabimus in doctrina de DEO. Secundo, ad removendam & excludendam omnem potentiam, quae imperfectionem aliquam arguit. Tria autem sunt potentiarum genera, quae ob imperfectionem suam DEO tribui nequeunt: nimirum potentia objectiva, quae nihil est aliud, quam rei producibilitas a causis suis: secundo, potentia passiva, quae rebus competit quatenus possunt ab agente aliquo pati & transmutari: tertio, potentia ad non esse. Prima potentia est rerum non existentium, ideoque DEO qui necessario existit, nec unquam potuit non existere, attribui nequit; duae posteriores sunt rerum existentium quidem, sed mutabilium & passibilium: DEUS autem est immutabilis, & impassibilis. At potentiae activae longe alia est ratio, nam potentia activa, ut bene observarunt Metaphysici, potius virtutis vel facultatis nomen meretur, quam potentiae: nam unumquodque agit in quantum est in actu, unde ipsa vis agendi actualitas quaedam est. Sed inquiet aliquis: omnis potentia est suo actu imperfectior: quicquid autem est imperfectum, vel absolute, vel comparative, a DEO removendum est. Respondetur, potentiam etiam activam in creaturis saepenumero esse imperfectiorem suo actu, idque quia creaturae perfectio in operatione & exercitio potentiae est posita, estque perfectior cum agit, quam cum non agit: at DEUS non ita se habet, ejus enim summa & infinita perfectio, seu beatitudo, in eo est posita, quod sit DEUS, ideoque non melius aut perfectius se habet, cum agit, quam cum non agit.

3. Ens constans ex potentia & actu, est Ens finitum actu existens in mundo: dicitur autem ejusmodi ens, constare ex actu & potentia, seu esse partim actuale, partim potentiale, ob duas rationes: Primo, quia in entibus finitis variae reperiuntur compositiones, nimirum ex genere & differentia, ex materia & forma, ex partibus integralibus, ex essentia & existentia; ex essentia existente & subsistentia illi superaddita, ex subjecto & accidente. In omnibus autem his compositionibus, (ea sola excepta quae est ex partibus integrantibus) est unum principium potentiale & receptivum, quod ob id appellatur potentia, alterum actuale & perfectivum, quod ob id dicitur actus: prioris generis principium in omni compositione substernitur, & posterioris generis principium ei superadditur. Hinc patet entia finita recte dici composita ex potentia & actu. Secunda ratio est haec: Entia finita, quamvis actu existant, & sic aliquem actum & perfectionem habeant, non tamen sunt mere actualia & perfecta, sed habent tria illa potentiarum genera imperfectionem arguentium. Primo enim priusquam existunt, habent objectivam illam potentiam ad existendum. Secundo cum existunt, habent potentiam passivam, & receptivam novorum accidentium. Tertio, habent potentiam ad non esse: possunt enim a prima causa aboleri, & in nihilum redigi.
